stem.text: Fig. 8.1 is a diagram of a sensory neurone.

stem.caption: Fig. 8.1
stem.alt: Diagram of a sensory neurone drawn left to right. At the left end a cluster of oval structures labelled A sits at the tip of a short branched dendrite. A long myelinated fibre (labelled 'myelin sheath' under a bracket) leads to a cell body (with its nucleus shown) part way along, then continues as another myelinated fibre ending in a branching set of terminal structures at the right, labelled B.

stem.text: Name the type of cell represented by cell A.

points.text: receptor ;

explanation.text: Structure A is at the sensory ending of the neurone, where stimuli are detected, so it represents a (sensory) receptor cell.

reasoningChain: A is at the dendrite end of a sensory neurone, which is where stimuli are detected: this identifies it as a receptor.

inferredMistakes.text: Naming the whole neurone (sensory neurone) rather than the receptor cell structure A specifically represents.

stem.text: Name a type of cell that forms a synapse with structure B.

points.text: intermediate neurone ; A relay neurone / motor neurone

explanation.text: Structure B is at the axon terminal of the sensory neurone, so the cell synapsing with it is the next neurone in the reflex/sensory pathway: an intermediate (relay) neurone, or a motor neurone.

reasoningChain: A sensory neurone's axon terminal synapses with the next neurone in the pathway, which is typically an intermediate neurone.

inferredMistakes.text: Naming another sensory neurone, when a sensory neurone's output synapses onward with an intermediate or motor neurone, not another sensory neurone.

stem.text: Name the cells that form the myelin sheath.

points.text: Schwann ;

explanation.text: The myelin sheath around a neurone's axon is formed by Schwann cells, which wrap repeatedly around the axon.

reasoningChain: Recall that Schwann cells are the cells that wrap around neurone axons to form the myelin sheath.

stem.text: State and explain the differences in the transmission of impulses between myelinated and unmyelinated neurones.

points.text: myelinated neurone faster (impulse transmission) ; ora
myelin (sheath), insulates (the axon) / prevents movement of ions ;
nodes of Ranvier / gaps with no myelin sheath, have voltage-gated channels
alternatives: nodes of Ranvier / gaps with no myelin sheath, allow movement of ions ;

points.text: depolarisation / action potential, occurs only at nodes of Ranvier / gaps with no myelin sheath ; ora
action potentials jump from node to node / saltatory conduction ; ora
longer local circuits / local circuits occur between nodes ; ora

explanation.text: The key difference is speed: impulses travel faster in myelinated neurones than in unmyelinated ones. This is because the myelin sheath insulates the axon, preventing ion movement across the membrane where it is present. Ion channels (and so depolarisation/action potentials) only occur at the nodes of Ranvier, the gaps between myelin segments. As a result, the action potential appears to jump from node to node (saltatory conduction), supported by longer local circuits between nodes, which is much faster than the node-by-node depolarisation that happens continuously along an unmyelinated axon.

reasoningChain: State the difference: myelinated is faster than unmyelinated.
Explain why: myelin insulates the axon so ions cannot cross it.
Ion channels, and so depolarisation, are restricted to the nodes of Ranvier.
This produces saltatory conduction (jumping between nodes) via longer local circuits, which is faster than continuous conduction.

inferredMistakes.text: Stating 'myelinated is faster' without explaining the mechanism (insulation forcing ion channels/depolarisation to the nodes, producing saltatory conduction), losing the explanation marks.

stem.text: Opioids are therapeutic drugs that are used to relieve pain. Morphine is an example of an opioid. It affects the functioning of synapses.
Fig. 8.2 is a diagram of a cholinergic synapse.

stem.caption: Fig. 8.2
stem.alt: Diagram of a cholinergic synapse. An arrow labelled 'pain stimulus' points down into the presynaptic neurone, a bulb-shaped ending containing several small oval vesicles. On the right of the presynaptic membrane, 'opioid receptor' and, below it, 'ion channel A' are labelled with lines pointing to small structures on the membrane. On the left, 'presynaptic neurone' labels the whole bulb. Below is the postsynaptic neurone, a wider curved structure. 'ion channel B' labels a structure at the top centre where the two neurones meet; on the right, 'opioid receptor' and, below it, 'ion channel C' label structures on the postsynaptic membrane; on the left, 'postsynaptic neurone' labels the whole structure.

stem.text: With reference to Fig. 8.2, describe the differences between ion channel A and ion channel B.

points.text: A voltage-gated and B ligand-gated / not voltage-gated
alternatives: A opens in response to, depolarisation / arrival of an action potential and B opens in response to binding of, acetylcholine / neurotransmitter ;

points.text: A for calcium ions and B for sodium ions ;

explanation.text: Ion channel A is on the presynaptic membrane and is voltage-gated: it opens when an action potential (depolarisation) arrives, letting calcium ions in. Ion channel B is on the postsynaptic membrane and is ligand-gated: it opens when acetylcholine (the neurotransmitter) binds to it, letting sodium ions in.

reasoningChain: A is presynaptic and opens due to the arriving action potential (voltage-gated), allowing Ca2+ in.
B is postsynaptic and opens when acetylcholine binds to it (ligand-gated), allowing Na+ in.

inferredMistakes.text: Mixing up which channel lets in which ion, or describing both channels as voltage-gated, missing that the postsynaptic channel responds to neurotransmitter binding, not voltage.

stem.text: Morphine binds to the opioid receptor in the presynaptic membrane. This stops the ion channel A from opening.
Suggest and describe the effects of the binding of morphine to this opioid receptor on the functioning of the cholinergic synapse.

points.text: no Ca2+ enter (presynaptic, knob / neurone) ;
vesicles do not, move towards / fuse with, presynaptic membrane ;
no, ACh / neurotransmitter, released
ACh / neurotransmitter, does not bind to, receptor / ion channel B ;
Na+ does not enter postsynaptic neurone / ion channel B does not open ;
postsynaptic membrane not depolarised

explanation.text: Because ion channel A cannot open, Ca2+ cannot enter the presynaptic neurone. Without the calcium influx, synaptic vesicles cannot move to and fuse with the presynaptic membrane, so no acetylcholine (ACh) is released by exocytosis. With no ACh released, none binds to the receptor/ion channel B on the postsynaptic membrane, so channel B does not open and Na+ cannot enter the postsynaptic neurone. The postsynaptic membrane is therefore not depolarised, no action potential is generated there, and the impulse (pain signal) is not transmitted across the synapse.

reasoningChain: Blocking ion channel A stops Ca2+ entering the presynaptic neurone.
No Ca2+ means vesicles cannot fuse with the presynaptic membrane.
No ACh is released by exocytosis.
No ACh means ion channel B (ligand-gated) does not open on the postsynaptic membrane.
No Na+ entry means no depolarisation, no action potential, and the pain impulse is blocked.

inferredMistakes.text: Jumping straight to 'pain is not transmitted' without describing the chain of events (calcium entry → vesicle fusion → ACh release → channel B opening → depolarisation) that earns the marks.

stem.text: Morphine also binds to the opioid receptor in the postsynaptic membrane. This results in the opening of ion channel C, allowing potassium ions to diffuse out of the cell.
Suggest how this would affect the synapse.

points.text: inside more negative (charge)
alternatives: membrane hyperpolarised / membrane potential decreases / potential difference increases ;

points.text: harder to / cannot, reach threshold ;
no depolarisation of membrane / harder to depolarise membrane
alternatives: no / fewer / harder to generate, action potentials / impulses ;

explanation.text: K+ diffusing out of the postsynaptic neurone makes the inside of the cell more negative than normal (the membrane hyperpolarises). This takes the membrane potential further from the threshold needed to trigger an action potential, so it becomes harder (or impossible) to depolarise the membrane enough to generate an action potential — fewer impulses get through.

reasoningChain: K+ leaving the cell makes the inside more negative (hyperpolarisation).
This moves the membrane potential further from threshold.
It becomes harder to depolarise the membrane and generate an action potential.

inferredMistakes.text: Confusing hyperpolarisation with depolarisation, i.e. saying K+ efflux makes it easier to fire an action potential, when it actually makes the membrane more negative and less likely to reach threshold.
